title: Electrochemistry: Electrode Potential and the Nernst Equation
subcategory: Electrochemistry — Electrode Potential, EMF, Nernst Equation, Conductance

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Electrochemistry

summary: Standard electrode potentials (measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode) predict a galvanic cell's EMF and reaction feasibility; the Nernst equation extends this to non-standard conditions, and molar conductivity trends distinguish strong from weak electrolytes.
explanation: Standard electrode potential (E°) is measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, arbitrarily assigned E° = 0.00 V), and tabulated as STANDARD REDUCTION potentials by convention — a more positive E° means a stronger tendency to be reduced (a better oxidising agent). For a galvanic cell, standard EMF = E°cathode(reduction) − E°anode(reduction) — using both values as REDUCTION potentials, a very common exam trap being to wrongly reverse the anode's sign twice. A positive cell EMF (equivalently, negative ΔG° = −nFE°cell) confirms the cell reaction is spontaneous as written. The Nernst equation, Ecell = E°cell − (RT/nF) ln Q (or the base-10, 298 K simplified form using 0.0591/n log Q), extends electrode/cell potential to NON-standard concentrations/pressures, explaining why a cell's measured EMF changes as the reaction proceeds and concentrations shift away from standard 1 M/1 atm conditions. At equilibrium, Ecell = 0, and this directly links E°cell to the equilibrium constant K. Molar conductivity (Λm = κ/C, where κ is specific conductance) INCREASES with dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes, but for a very different reason in each: for strong electrolytes, it increases only slightly and levels off at a finite, measurable limiting value (Λm°) because ionic interactions weaken with dilution; for weak electrolytes, it increases sharply and continuously (never quite reaching a directly measurable plateau) because the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION itself increases with dilution, producing more ions. Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that at infinite dilution, each ion contributes a fixed, characteristic value to the total molar conductivity regardless of the other ion present — this lets Λm° for a WEAK electrolyte be calculated indirectly by combining known Λm° values of strong electrolytes, since it can't be measured directly by extrapolation for a weak electrolyte.
commonMisconceptions: Reversing sign conventions incorrectly when calculating cell EMF — the standard formula uses BOTH electrode potentials as reduction potentials (cathode minus anode); manually flipping the anode's sign AND then also subtracting is a double-negative error many students make.

Assuming molar conductivity increasing with dilution means the SAME thing for strong and weak electrolytes — for strong electrolytes it's a modest increase toward a directly measurable limit; for weak electrolytes it's a steep, theoretically-unbounded-by-direct-measurement increase due to increasing dissociation.

Believing a negative standard electrode potential means a species cannot be reduced at all — it only means that species is a WEAKER oxidising agent than H⁺/H₂ (the SHE reference); reduction can still occur under sufficiently favourable non-standard conditions or with a strong enough reducing partner.
examples: In a Daniell cell (Zn/Zn²⁺ ‖ Cu²⁺/Cu), zinc (more negative E°) is oxidised at the anode while copper ions are reduced at the cathode, giving a standard EMF of about 1.10 V.
A dead battery can sometimes work again briefly after resting, because as the reaction proceeds, concentrations of reactants/products shift, changing the EMF per the Nernst equation.
genZNote: Cell EMF = cathode's ego minus anode's ego, both measured as reduction potentials — no exceptions.
